title: Venture capital firm Pelorus to fund nascent startups in thriving St. John’s tech scene
html:
Chris Moyer and Sarah Murphy of St. John's NL-based Pelorus on Oct. 28. Pelorus has had good fortune on the deal flow front since raising its first, $14-million fund in 2014, mostly backed by the province.Alex Stead/The Globe and Mail

Pelorus Venture Capital has played a pivotal role financing companies in the thriving technology scene of St. John’s. Now it’s extending its reach to help new startups get off the ground in a bid to keep entrepreneurs from leaving the Rock.

The Atlantic Canadian financier, which has raised $42.5-million for its third fund, has set aside $1-million to back fourth-year or recently graduated, entrepreneurially minded engineering students from hometown Memorial University. Pelorus, which usually invests $500,000 to $1-million per company, will cut cheques as small as $50,000 under the strategy for startups, some just months old.

“We saw a gap in the market, and because we’ve never been afraid to go early, we’ve decided to go even earlier,” said Pelorus managing partner Chris Moyer. The idea, he said, is to persuade promising students to start companies at home rather than depart for high-paying Silicon Valley jobs.

It’s part of an effort within the tightknit local tech community to build on its out-of-the-way success, despite challenges such as the area’s remoteness and sparse population. Fraud-detection software maker Verafin, which was sold to Nasdaq Inc. in 2020 for US$2.75-billion, is the best-known local tech company. More recently, engineering software maker CoLab AI Inc. and legal AI software vendor Spellbook have also grown rapidly, attracted global investors and generated tens of millions of dollars in revenues apiece.

Local entrepreneurs who’ve succeeded have helped their peers, including CoLab CEO Adam Keating. He has mentored young entrepreneurs and co-founded Memorial’s Student Design Hub for students competing in engineering competitions.

“The biggest constraint here is getting the next batch of people locally to believe they can” start tech companies at home, Mr. Keating said. “We have an awareness problem still. As much as this has worked and people know about us, they still think, ‘I can’t do that.’ We need to show them they can.”

That is the point of Pelorus’s new strategy, which “is an experiment,” said partner Sarah Murphy. “We see really bright students at Memorial. They have ideas. We want to give them an opportunity to test out entrepreneurship.” It’s also “a great opportunity to get in very early and be there so that you have really good deal flow.”

Pelorus has had good fortune on the deal flow front since raising its first, $14-million fund in 2014, mostly backed by the province. Its early local bets – including investments in CoLab, Spellbook and smart thermostat maker Mysa − turned Pelorus into one of Canada’s top-performing venture capital firms. It is aiming to raise $50-million for its third fund.

It has backed two local companies from the new strategy so far: Clace Research and OmaScan. The founders of both AI-enabled companies, launched in 2026, were introduced to Pelorus by Mr. Keating.

Clace founder Joshua Kattapuram came from southern India to study computer science at Memorial because international student fees were low and he had family in the area. After working as an intern on the trading desk at Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan in 2024, he started a society for Memorial students interested in quantitative finance. He graduated last spring.

When Mr. Kattapuram decided this year to become an entrepreneur, Pelorus’s principals were keen to invest, but he held them off; he wanted to make sure he had an idea worth backing first. By the summer his plan was afoot to build an AI-enabled financial advisory firm for lenders to data-centre owners, to assess the creditworthiness of the projects. Clace built a product that uses AI to ingest heaps of data, including satellite imagery, permitting information and internet traffic flows from centres, to inform its analysis.

Last month it landed its first client, a large New York lender. “The fact that they’re willing to take a product from a random company in Newfoundland with a team of three people probably means there is real demand for something like this,” Mr. Kattapuram said. This fall the company raised US$200,000, mostly from Pelorus, with the goal of making Clace “the Moody’s of AI infrastructure,” he said.

Mr. Kattapuram credited the Pelorus team for being hands-on and doing what they can to help, he said. He has no plans to relocate the business, as “people are nice” in St. John’s and the costs of labour and office space are relatively low. “I’m a believer that environment shapes you. The startups here typically work hard, and no one is here to lose. There’s no real reason or advantage to relocate.”
summary: Earmarks money from new funds to entice students to start companies at home – instead of leaving for jobs in Silicon Valley
